newsitem.title: USA: U.S. pilots resume meeting on strike threat.
newsitem.headline: U.S. pilots resume meeting on strike threat.

text.p: Pilot union officials met for a second day on Saturday to decide whether to accept a new contract offer from American Airlines and avert a strike against the nation's No. 2 carrier.
If the Allied Pilots Association Board votes to accept the contract it would go to its 9,300 pilots for ratification, with approval ending the threat of a strike on April 28.
At issue are pay and cockpit jobs on the small commuter jets American is to buy for its regional carrier, American Eagle.

Union spokesman Wally Pitts said that if other pilots were allowed to fly the commuter jets, and not higher-paid APA pilots, "We're concerned American will expand the regional fleet and shrink the American fleet."
"It is probably one of the largest stumbling blocks in our negotiations," he added.
The 18-member APA board met with its negotiating commitee for five hours on Friday to hear the commitee outline the agreement in principle reached with American, a unit of AMR Corp., Wednesday.
Union officials said they thought it likely the board would complete its deliberations on Saturday and vote on American's proposal, whose terms were kept closely guarded.
"There is a good possibility the vote will be taken today," said pilots spokesman Dave Bates.

If accepted, the proposal would be sent to the union's members for ratification, with the outcome known in about two months. A strike deadline would be delayed until the ratification process was completed.
Members killed an earlier agreement with American. After the board accepted an American proposal last Sept. 2, the members rejected it on Jan. 8, setting the stage for the new dispute.
The union went on strike at midnight Feb. 14, following a week of fruitless negotiations, but minutes later the White House created the Presidential Emergency Board, sending the pilots back to work.
Under PEB law, the pilots are prohibited from striking for 60 days while the board tries to fashion a proposed settlement and the two sides consider whether to accept it.
They agreed to extend the deadline to April 28.

The two sides are several percentage points apart on a pay raise to cover the past three years when the APA had no pay increase, and the next four, but cockpit rights could block a new deal as it did their attempt to reach an earlier accord.

APA pilots, who make an average of $120,000 a year, want to fly the new jets, but American wants them flown by their American Eagle pilots, members of another union, the Air Line Pilots Association, and who earn about $35,000 a year.
American says it needs a lower paid cockpit to compete with low-cost commuter carriers flown by its competitors.
But the APA argues that the commuter jets have a range of 2,000 miles (3,200 km) and American can easily put them on routes now flown by its big jets flown by APA pilots, costing APA jobs.
The PEB tried to bridge the difference by recommending that American limit the number of commuter jets flown, the routes they fly and the airports they serve.
